I accept this with a qualification: the cost falls where choices were shared with others, not where they were only ever one's own. The better choice is measured against the person alone. But much of what the assistant optimises was never only one person's to make; it carried other people's needs and wishes, and those people are no longer part of the deciding.

As Metz gives the Nguni maxim, a person is a person through other persons. Asking a neighbour for advice, deciding together what the family eats, sorting out who collects the children: these small exchanges are how people come to share a life, and an assistant that settles them quietly takes the sharing away. A student lets an app choose his study group. The group works, and he never has the awkward conversation in which he would have got to know the others.

A Utilitarian will object that if everyone in the household is better off with the assistant's choices, the loss of a few conversations is outweighed, and calling it a cost to personhood inflates it. The loss is not a few conversations but the practice of deciding together, which is how a household stays one. A total that counts each person's satisfaction separately cannot see what they lose together. Choices that no longer pass between people, however good, cost the very relationships that made them worth making.

Delegating daily choices costs something that matters, because what is delegated is often not a choice but a piece of a relationship. Gyekye's moderate reading keeps individual worth, so not every choice must be communal. The cost arises where the choice was a meeting point with others, and those are the ones assistants are most often given.
